scope: Bounded primary-source review for 4D-ball slices, orthographic projection, center/interior/boundary/empty distinctions, and a declared representation-ambiguity construction
execution_policy: Read-only source inspection. No implementation, browser run, deployment, external communication, human study, Gate 5 research, or publication.

primary_sources.title: Lecture 11: High Dimensional Geometry, Curse of Dimensionality, Dimension Reduction
primary_sources.author: Sanjeev Arora (Princeton University, COS 521)
pins: PDF p. 1, lines 40–44 in fetched text: unit n-ball B_n is defined by sum_i x_i^2 <= 1.
PDF p. 1, lines 45–53 in fetched text: the x_1=1/2 hyperplane slice of the 4D ball is a 3-ball of radius sqrt(1−1/2^2), and every parallel slice is a ball.
supports: A hyperplane slice of the unit n-ball is an (n−1)-ball in the displayed 4D example.
The square-root radius law for the unit case; scaling and substitution give sqrt(R^2−s^2) for a 4D ball of radius R sliced at w=s.
does_not_support: The project's browser implementation, rendering backend, or display-camera contract.
A claim that a 3D movie uniquely identifies a 4D source or that extra physical dimensions exist.
The boundary/singleton/empty UI policy; those follow from the displayed inequality and the Toronto definitions below.
primary_sources.use_in_gate4: Primary source for the higher-dimensional ball definition and parallel-slice example underlying the analytic 4D-ball model.

primary_sources.title: Basic terminology and notation; Interior, boundary, and closure
primary_sources.author: University of Toronto, MATH 237Y1 analysis notes
pins: Lines 17–22: open ball uses |x−a|<r, sphere uses |x−a|=r, and closed ball uses |x−a|<=r.
Lines 28–38: interior, complement-interior, and boundary are defined by neighborhood conditions.
Lines 56–71: for an open ball, the interior is the ball and the boundary is the radius-r sphere.
supports: Keeping a solid ball, its spherical boundary, and the equality sphere mathematically distinct.
The neighborhood meaning of interior and boundary used to explain why the nondegenerate slice has a solid interior and spherical boundary.
does_not_support: The exact 4D slice radius formula; that is derived by substitution from the Princeton ball equation.
A browser or human-comprehension result, arbitrary-shape reconstruction, or a physical extra-dimension claim.
primary_sources.use_in_gate4: Primary terminology reference for the ball/sphere distinction and explicit boundary handling.

derived_checks.formula: B^4_R ∩ {w=s} = {(x,y,z,s): x^2+y^2+z^2 <= R^2−s^2}; radius sqrt(R^2−s^2) for |s|<R
derived_checks.derivation: Substitute w=s into x^2+y^2+z^2+w^2<=R^2. The Princeton source gives the unit-radius parallel-slice case; scaling gives general R.
derived_checks.status: direct derivation under the declared Euclidean closed-ball model

derived_checks.formula: s=0 gives radius R; 0<|s|<R gives positive radius; |s|=R gives a singleton; |s|>R gives empty
derived_checks.derivation: Analyze the residual radius-squared R^2−s^2 and the equality/inequality set. Toronto's definitions keep solid interiors and spherical boundaries separate.
derived_checks.status: direct derivation; singleton is a degenerate intersection, not an ordinary zero-radius rendering

derived_checks.derivation: Dropping w^2 proves inclusion in B^3_R; every (x,y,z) in B^3_R lifts to (x,y,z,0) in B^4_R. An orthogonal source rotation preserves the centered ball.
derived_checks.status: direct set-theoretic derivation; display scale and camera remain separate recorded variables

derived_checks.claim: Stored 3D animation reproduces a selected projection movie
derived_checks.formula: Given m(t)=P R(t) q(t), define a stored 3D trajectory a(t)=m(t)
derived_checks.derivation: The stored trajectory has exactly the same declared 3D frame output as the chosen movie while carrying no fourth coordinate.
derived_checks.status: constructive counterexample derived for Gate 4; not quoted or attributed to either external source

limits: The slice result assumes a centered Euclidean solid 4D ball and a coordinate hyperplane w=s; translated or tilted planes require the corresponding distance-to-center substitution.
The orthographic image result assumes the coordinate projection with no automatic rescaling; perspective projection or a display transform may change apparent size.

The ambiguity construction concerns a bounded class of stored 3D trajectories/frame sequences matching one declared movie; it is not a theorem about all representations or arbitrary shape reconstruction.
Mathematical checks do not establish that a viewer can understand an unfamiliar slice, distinguish projection from slice, or infer source dimension from a movie.
